soil-fert-250.title: How surface manure loses its nitrogen to the air
soil-fert-250.text: Leave manure on the surface and its nitrogen starts to vanish within a day. Ammonium and urea turn to ammonia gas as the manure dries and are lost to the air. About half of dairy manure N comes from urine urea, which converts to the ammonium that is almost all of its readily available N (see {{ref:soil-fert-246}}). Surface-left dairy manure loses about 25% of its N after one day and 45% after four days, around 70% of the readily available N. Half an inch of rain soon after application leaches ammonium in. Incorporating the manure in spring helps, and fall injection of liquid manure greatly reduces loss compared with broadcasting. Surface manure also risks nutrient runoff to surface waters.

soil-fert-251.title: Timing manure to the crop
soil-fert-251.text:
Manure works best when it lands near the time the crop needs nutrients. For annual crops, apply in one dose just before tillage so it is incorporated fast. Injection close to planting cuts runoff and erosion risk. Fall application in humid climates lets ammonium convert to nitrate that leaches or denitrifies. A three-year New York study found about twice the N leaching from fall as from spring liquid manure on corn silage.

Grass hay is constantly N deficient. It does best with about 50-75 pounds available N in early spring and after each harvest, though wet early-spring soils risk compaction. Spreading on frozen or snow-covered ground is legal in most states but poor practice. Injection into a shallow 2-4 inch frozen layer avoids runoff. The rates themselves are the subject of {{ref:soil-fert-249}}.

soil-water-003.title: How rain and runoff carry soil away
soil-water-003.text:
Almost 36 billion tons of soil are lost to water every year, according to a global model. Water erosion is the removal of soil by rainfall and by the surface runoff it produces, a form of {{ref:soil-water-001}}. It begins with the rain itself. Raindrops bombard aggregates and detach small particles that are easily transported, by splash or by water running downhill, to a low area where they are deposited.

Runoff, the flow described in {{ref:soil-water-019}}, begins when the soil is saturated or when rain falls faster than water can infiltrate (see {{ref:soil-water-180}}). Runoff with enough flow energy carries loosened soil particles down the slope as sediment. Rain and runoff cause four main types of erosion, in rising severity: splash, sheet, rill and gully erosion. Concentrated runoff cuts small channels called rills. If runoff keeps deepening them, they may grow into gullies, a gully being a rill too deep for tillage equipment to smooth.

Sheet and rill erosion cause most soil erosion. The damage is not evenly spread, either. Water erosion removes soil mainly from the middle and lower parts of a slope rather than from hilltops.

soil-water-105.title: Soil loss tolerance: how much erosion is too much
soil-water-105.text:
How fast can a soil lose its top layer and still farm well forever? Soil loss tolerance, the T value, answers in tons per acre per year: the maximum average yearly loss that still lets a soil sustain current production economically and indefinitely. T values range from 1 to 5. Devised by the US Soil Conservation Service, the idea rests on the minimum rate of loss that would deplete organic matter and harm crop productivity. It is calculated with the formula T=υQρC+R(1−C). In 1961-1962 US soil groups were given T values of 2 to 6, later adjusted to 1 to 5, and conservation management adopted it from the mid-1960s.

In depth terms, a soil deeper than 5 feet has a T of 5 tons per acre per year (11 metric tons per hectare), about 0.03 inch of depth a year, or 1 inch in 33 years. T is lower for shallow soils: with rooting depth under 10 inches it equals 0.006 inch a year, or 1 inch in 167 years. By 2007, 99 million acres, 28% of US cropland, were eroding faster than T, down from 169 million acres, 40% of cropland, in 1982.

The value's validity is questioned. Critics note that T values vary across space, may not hold where soluble carbonates abound, as in karst, and should be weighed against actual soil loss. {{ref:soil-water-001}} is the loss it measures.

soil-water-298.title: Marine clay: soft sediment from the sea floor
soil-water-298.text:
Marine clays are fine-grained sedimentary deposits made mostly of {{ref:soil-found-040}} minerals that build up in coastal environments. They derive from weathered continental rocks carried to the ocean, where they settle and consolidate on the seabed. They commonly contain {{ref:soil-chem-094}}, {{ref:soil-chem-091}}, {{ref:soil-chem-088}} and chlorite, plus varying silt, organic matter and biogenic material. Saline deposition shapes their structure and bonding, often giving high natural water content and low permeability.

Seawater's excess ions make deposited clay flocculate into a loose, open structure (see {{ref:soil-phys-006}}). Once dried by falling sea level, it admits water easily. That fragile structure makes marine clays highly sensitive: they can lose much of their strength when disturbed. One more clue is stratigraphic. Marine clay lying over peat may mark a marine flooding surface, reflecting landward coastal shift during relative sea-level rise.

soil-water-299.title: Why clay clumps where rivers meet the sea
soil-water-299.text: Fine silt and clay stay suspended longer than sand. Small, negatively charged clay particles can resist settling altogether and stay suspended, producing turbidity. Flocculation is the process by which fine particles in water clump together into flocs, as in {{ref:soil-phys-006}}. In estuaries, changing physicochemical conditions from river to sea trigger flocculation and siltation, a main cause of harbour dredging. Organic matter plays a major role by adhering to marine clay particles. The exchange cations on the particles (sodium, potassium, calcium) set their arrangement and properties.

soil-water-300.title: Building on marine clay
soil-water-300.text:
Marine clay is a geotechnical challenge because the soil is open, sensitive and weak under load. It is sensitive to weathering, which affects support under loads and limits bearing capacity and service life. Pavements over it lose durability and cost more over their life. The worst case is {{ref:soil-water-071}}: very unstable, it liquefies and flows when saturated, causing mass wasting.

Ground improvement techniques can handle the problems, and marine clay can be stabilized by mixing with cement and fly ash in set proportions. The same material has uses. Marine clays serve as low-permeability landfill liners and adsorb contaminants, and they have long been used for heat-resistant ceramics. The material itself is described in {{ref:soil-water-298}}.

soil-phys-030.title: Gilgai: the self-made hills and pools of cracking clay
soil-phys-030.text:
In some clay landscapes the ground ripples into mounds and hollows, and the hollows fill with small seasonal pools. This microrelief is gilgai. It forms in expanding clay soils, notably the {{ref:soil-class-106}}, through repeated swelling when wet and shrinkage when dry, a churning called {{ref:soil-form-123}} that heaves underlying material to the surface. The soil cracks when dry, and loose material fills the cracks. On re-wetting the soil is forced sideways, raising a mound between cracks and a depression at each crack.

The pattern feeds itself. Depressions hold water, swell more and crack more, and the cracks channel water deep, exaggerating the pattern each cycle. Pools are commonly a few metres across and under 30 cm deep, though some are several metres deep and up to 100 m across. Gilgais occur worldwide on cracking clays with marked wet and dry seasons. Crayfish and ants magnify the forms by bioturbation. Frost polygons of cold regions look similar but form by freeze-thaw.

The movement is costly. It damages foundations, roads and railways, and the undulations hamper harvesting. Field surveys treat gilgai, along with deep shrinkage cracks, as a visible sign of the {{ref:soil-phys-029}} behind {{ref:soil-phys-028}}. One source differs on the word: USDA soil taxonomy's soil-order list calls the deep cracks that form in drying Vertisols gilgai.

soil-agri-193.title: What a rotation does to soil organic matter
soil-agri-193.text:
Plow up virgin forest or prairie and plant row crops, and organic matter drops rapidly for five to ten years, until a low equilibrium is reached that holds if practices stay unchanged. Under a rotation (see {{ref:soil-agri-004}}), crop type, yield, root mass, harvested portion and residue management together set {{ref:soil-found-045}}. Switching to grass or grass-legume sod raises it, but more slowly than the loss under continuous tillage.

Long experiments show the spread. In a 60-year Missouri experiment, continuous corn lost over 9 inches of topsoil (21 tons per acre a year) and ended with 1.2% organic matter, against 2.2% under unfertilized timothy. A six-year rotation kept about 70% of the timothy topsoil. In eastern Canada, continuous corn added about 100 pounds of organic matter per acre yearly, corn-alfalfa 500, four-year alfalfa 800; 3% organic matter is about 60,000 pounds per acre.

Perennial forages slow decomposition by reducing disturbance and add organic matter from sod roots, part of which die each year. Older grass roots die even during the growing season. Gains have a ceiling: they plateau once mineral surfaces are saturated and the soil is highly aggregated, however much residue, manure or compost is added.

Life in the soil follows. In semiarid Oregon, total microorganisms under a two-year wheat-fallow system were about 25% of the amount under pasture. Moldboard plow tillage decreases earthworm and other soil organism populations, and including perennial forages enhances the diversity effect.

soil-agri-180.title: Choosing a cover crop for the job
soil-agri-180.text:
Different cover crops are grown for different primary purposes. Grasses such as cereal rye and oats catch and cycle nutrients. Legumes such as hairy vetch and red clover fix nitrogen with Rhizobium as green manures (see {{ref:soil-fert-026}}). Fast-growing competitive species such as buckwheat and sorghum-sudangrass smother weeds. Brassicas such as mustards and radishes biofumigate pests with glucosinolates and isothiocyanates. Strong-rooted crops such as cereal rye, radishes, hairy vetch and alfalfa loosen compacted soil, while sorghum-sudangrass, cereal rye and sunn hemp build biomass and organic matter.

Ecologists separate canopy functions (aboveground biomass) from root functions (belowground biomass), and choice can follow the traits wanted. Grass cover crops are more likely than legumes to increase {{ref:soil-found-045}}, and some grow as much or more biomass underground as above. Hairy vetch or crimson clover may yield 1.5 to over 4 tons dry weight per acre, mature cereal rye 3-5 tons, and early-terminated crops as little as half a ton.

The gains are measurable. A five-year California clover experiment raised organic matter in the top 2 inches from 1.3% to 2.6%. Pooled experiments found cover crops raised organic matter 8.5% over original levels and soil nitrogen 12.8%.

soil-agri-179.title: Mineral wool as a growing medium
soil-agri-179.text: Mineral wool is a fibrous material spun or drawn from molten rock or slag. Among other uses, it is a hydroponic growth medium, a relative of the {{ref:soil-agri-031}}. Stone wool is made by blowing air or steam through molten rock at about 1600 C, giving fine intertwined fibres 2 to 6 micrometres across. Products can be engineered to hold large amounts of water and air for root growth and nutrient uptake, and the fibres give mechanical support. Its naturally high pH makes it unsuitable at first, so it needs conditioning, for example pre-soaking in nutrient solution at pH 5.5 until it stops bubbling.

soil-agri-186.title: When cover crops feed the next crop, or starve it
soil-agri-186.text:
A cover crop can feed the next crop or deliberately lower available nitrogen at season end to cut losses. A productive legume grown to bud stage can make 70 to well over 100 pounds of nitrogen per acre available. Hairy vetch and crimson clover are frequent choices. How much arrives depends on growth stage, biomass and nitrogen content. Small deep-green plants contain over 3 percent N but little total N.

Grasses go the other way. Cereal rye N falls below 1 percent with a C:N ratio of 80 or more at maturity. At about 1.5-2 percent N, soil organisms use all the nitrogen and little reaches the next crop.

soil-agri-182.title: Grass cover crops and what they scavenge
soil-agri-182.text: Grass cover crops include annual cereals (rye, wheat, triticale, barley, oats), forage grasses such as ryegrass, and warm-season grasses such as sorghum-sudangrass. Their fibrous root systems scavenge leftover nutrients, especially nitrogen, and some establish rapidly to greatly reduce erosion. They produce large amounts of residue and roots that add organic matter, and the residue helps suppress weed germination. Cereal rye grows in late fall and early spring as a catch crop and soil conditioner in cool regions. In Maryland it is widely used to cut nutrient loading into the Chesapeake Bay.
